lesson.title: Where Mutations Come From: Mutagens and the Sources of DNA Damage
lesson.summary: Mutagens are physical or chemical agents that damage DNA or interfere with its accurate replication, raising the mutation rate above the low background level of spontaneous errors.
lesson.body:
Point mutations and frameshift mutations do not appear from nowhere. Some arise spontaneously, from the ordinary chemistry of DNA and the occasional imperfection of replication. Others are caused by mutagens: physical or chemical agents from the environment that damage DNA directly or interfere with its accurate copying, raising the mutation rate well above its normal spontaneous background level.

Physical mutagens include ultraviolet light and ionizing radiation. Ultraviolet light is absorbed by DNA and can cause two adjacent pyrimidine bases, most often two thymines, on the same strand to form a covalent bond with each other, creating a pyrimidine dimer that distorts the double helix and blocks DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase from moving past it unless it is repaired. Ionizing radiation, such as X-rays and gamma rays, carries enough energy to break the sugar phosphate backbone directly, producing single strand or, more seriously, double strand breaks, and it also generates reactive oxygen species in the cell that go on to damage bases chemically.

Chemical mutagens act by several distinct mechanisms. Base analogs, such as 5-bromouracil, are similar enough in shape to a normal base that DNA polymerase can incorporate them into a new strand in place of the real thing, but they mispair more readily than the base they replace, producing substitutions in later rounds of replication. Alkylating agents attach chemical groups directly onto bases, which can change their pairing behavior or destabilize the bond holding the base to the sugar phosphate backbone entirely, leading to a missing base. Deaminating agents, such as nitrous acid, chemically convert cytosine into uracil, a base that pairs like thymine rather than cytosine, so the next round of replication turns what was a C:G pair into a T:A pair, a permanent transition mutation. Intercalating agents are flat molecules that wedge themselves between stacked base pairs in the double helix, distorting its geometry enough that DNA polymerase tends to skip a base or insert an extra one when copying past the distortion, which makes intercalating agents a common cause of frameshift mutations specifically, rather than point mutations.

DNA is also damaged, and mutated, without any external mutagen at all. Purine bases occasionally detach from the sugar phosphate backbone spontaneously, a process called depurination, leaving a gap that replication may fill in incorrectly. Cytosine spontaneously deaminates to uracil at a low but steady rate even without a chemical mutagen. And DNA polymerase itself, despite its accuracy, occasionally inserts a mismatched base simply because a base briefly takes on an unusual, rare chemical form that pairs incorrectly for a moment.

Most of this damage never becomes a permanent mutation, because cells have layered systems for finding and fixing it before the next round of replication makes it permanent. DNA polymerase's own proofreading catches many errors as they happen. Mismatch repair scans newly replicated DNA for base pairs that do not fit the pairing rules and corrects them. Base excision repair removes single damaged or inappropriate bases, such as a deaminated cytosine, and replaces them correctly. Nucleotide excision repair removes bulkier distortions, such as ultraviolet induced pyrimidine dimers, by cutting out and replacing a short stretch of the damaged strand. A mutation, in the end, is DNA damage that escaped all of these systems and was copied into a permanent, heritable change in the sequence.
